The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $M$ be a compact smooth $3$-manifold. A properly embedded surface is **two-sided** if it has a product neighbourhood $F\times[-1,1]$ in $M$. A **compressing disk** for a two-sided surface $F$ is an embedded disk $D\subset M$ with $\operatorname{int}(D)\cap F=\varnothing$ and $\partial D$ an essential simple closed curve in $F$; $F$ is **incompressible** if it has no compressing disk. A **boundary-compressing disk** is an embedded disk $D$ with $\partial D=\alpha\cup\beta$, where $\alpha=D\cap F$ is an arc not cutting off a disk in $F$, $\beta=D\cap\partial M$, and $\operatorname{int}(D)$ misses $F\cup\partial M$; $F$ is **boundary-incompressible** if it has no such disk. A surface is **boundary-parallel** if it cobounds a product with a subsurface of $\partial M$, and it is **essential** if it is incompressible, boundary-incompressible, and not boundary-parallel. $M$ is **irreducible** if every embedded $2$-sphere in its interior bounds an embedded $3$-ball in $M$. An incompressible torus is boundary-parallel if it cobounds a product $T^2\times[0,1]$ with a component of $\partial M$; $M$ is **atoroidal** if every incompressible torus is boundary-parallel. A **Seifert fibration** is a decomposition into circles with local models given by fibered solid tori; in the model $(D^2\times S^1)/\langle(z,w)\mapsto(e^{2\pi i/q}z,e^{2\pi ip/q}w)\rangle$, where $\gcd(p,q)=1$, the core fiber has multiplicity $q$. Fibers of multiplicity $1$ are **regular** and those of multiplicity greater than $1$ are **exceptional**. A finite family of pairwise disjoint incompressible tori is a **JSJ system** if every component obtained by cutting $M$ along the family is atoroidal or Seifert-fibered. It is **inclusion-minimal** if no proper subfamily is a JSJ system. Atoroidal does not mean hyperbolic.

Let $B$ be a parametrized PL three-ball with a finite compatible PL manifold triangulation. Let $T\subset\operatorname{Int}B$ be the image of a PL embedding of the standard PL torus. Suppose $T$ is two-sided, meaning that it has a topological product neighborhood $T\times(-1,1)$ with the given central inclusion. Then $T$ has a finite compatible PL bicollar and an embedded PL disk $D\subset\operatorname{Int}B$ with $D\cap T=\partial D$ and $\partial D$ essential on $T$. No choice axiom is assumed.

The PL hypothesis on the torus is explicit. This result supplies no compatibility assertion for a torus given only by an unqualified topological embedding in the ball.

Let $Q$ be a compact piecewise-linear polyhedron with a fixed finite linear triangulation $T$. If $f:P\to Q$ is a piecewise-linear embedding of a compact piecewise-linear polyhedron, then some finite subdivision $T'$ of $T$ contains $f(P)$ as the realization of a subcomplex.

Each connected cutting torus lies wholly inside or wholly outside that sphere. If a torus lies inside $B$, its existing two-sided neighborhood can be shrunk into $\operatorname{Int}B$, by compactness and a common smaller product width. It remains a PL embedded torus there. [F3] supplies the compatible finite subdivisions needed for [F2], even if the original triangulation of $B$ was different from the one containing the torus.

Every interior PL sphere there therefore bounds a PL ball. This is precisely PL irreducibility; no smooth-ball or arbitrary-topological-marking claim entered.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. Let $p,q$ be coprime nonzero integers, let $K=T(p,q)$ be the oriented primitive slope curve in the standard Heegaard torus, and let $\rho_t(z_1,z_2)=(e^{2\pi i p t}z_1,e^{2\pi i q t}z_2)$ be the weighted circle action on the unit $S^3\subset\mathbb C^2$. Choose $N(K)$ to be a sufficiently small closed metric tube around the orbit $K$ for the round metric; this tube is invariant because $\rho_t$ is isometric and preserves $K$. Set $E_K=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)$. Let $x$ and $y$ be based generators of the fundamental groups of the two solid-torus pieces obtained by cutting $E_K$ along the annulus left on the Heegaard torus, oriented so that the annulus core maps to $x^p$ and $y^q$. Then

$$\pi_1(E_K)=\langle x,y\mid x^p=y^q\rangle.$$

The common element $h=x^p=y^q$ is central and represents a regular fiber of a Seifert fibration of $E_K$ over a disk. The fibration has two distinguished core fibers of multiplicities $|p|$ and $|q|$; a fiber of multiplicity one is regular, and a fiber of multiplicity greater than one is exceptional. Thus there are exactly two exceptional fibers when $|p|,|q|>1$, and one is regular when one absolute parameter is $1$.

For any integers $\alpha,\beta$ with $p\alpha+q\beta=1$, compatible based paths identify the positive normal-disk meridian and preferred longitude in the peripheral system as

$$\mu=y^\alpha x^\beta,\qquad \lambda=h\mu^{-pq}.$$

Here the positive meridian is the oriented boundary of a normal disk, and the preferred longitude has degree one around $K$ and maps to zero in $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$. Their homology classes form a basis of $H_1(\partial E_K;\mathbb Z)$, so both classes are primitive.

Let $X=U\cup V$, where $U$ and $V$ are open path-connected subsets of $X$, let $U\cap V$ be path-connected, and fix $x_0\in U\cap V$. For the inclusion-induced maps in the diagram

$$\pi_1(U,x_0)\longleftarrow\pi_1(U\cap V,x_0)\longrightarrow\pi_1(V,x_0),$$

the group $\pi_1(X,x_0)$, together with the two inclusion-induced homomorphisms, is a pushout ([[def-pushout-of-group-homomorphisms]]). Equivalently, the canonical homomorphism from any pushout $P$ of the displayed diagram to $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ is an isomorphism. No injectivity of either map from the overlap group is assumed.

Every element of $G\ast_KH$ has a unique normal form $s_1\cdots s_nk$ relative to fixed transversals. A normal word of positive length is nonidentity. The represented group and these conclusions are independent of the chosen transversals.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Every nonempty compact
connected boundaryless topological $2$-manifold is homeomorphic to exactly one
of the following types: the sphere $S^2$, a connected sum of $g\geq1$ tori,
or a connected sum of $k\geq1$ real projective planes. The connected sums here
are the explicit polygonal models with their chosen disk removals and boundary
gluings ([[def-connected-sum-of-compact-surfaces]]). The integer is unique
within its type. Equivalently, two such surfaces are homeomorphic if and only
if they have the same integral orientability and Euler characteristic.

The canonical one-face words are respectively the sphere digon $aa^{-1}$
(whose *reduced notation* is empty), the $g$-fold commutator word
$\prod_{i=1}^g a_i b_i a_i^{-1} b_i^{-1}$, and the $k$-fold square word
$\prod_{j=1}^k c_jc_j$. The empty notation is not an empty polygonal schema.

Assume full AC. Let $M$ be a compact connected irreducible Seifert-fibered $3$-manifold, and let $F\subset M$ be a connected, two-sided essential annulus or torus, neatly embedded at its boundary (the condition is vacuous for a torus). Then $F$ is ambient isotopic to either a vertical surface, meaning a union of regular fibers, or a horizontal surface, meaning a surface transverse to every fiber. For a horizontal surface $F$ with $n$ sheets over the base orbifold $B$ and exceptional-fiber multiplicities $q_1,\ldots,q_m$, the Euler characteristics satisfy
$$
\frac{\chi(F)}{n}=\chi(B)-\sum_{i=1}^m\left(1-\frac1{q_i}\right).
$$
If $F$ is two-sided and horizontal, cutting $M$ along $F$ gives an interval bundle over a surface.

For a smooth boundary-preimage embedding without the neatness condition, the same vertical-or-horizontal normal form is attained by a smooth isotopy of embeddings, fixed on the original boundary during its preliminary neatification, and by a topological ambient isotopy. The Euler count and interval-bundle conclusions apply to the resulting horizontal representative. A smooth ambient isotopy is asserted for the neat inputs above.

Assume full AC. Let $K$ be a nontrivial smooth knot with a specified companion solid torus $V=e(S^1\times D^2)$, let $P\subset\operatorname{int}(S^1\times D^2)$ be a pattern, and assume the outer torus of its pattern exterior $X_P$ has no compressing disk and is not product-parallel to the inner pattern torus. Let $T_c=\partial V=e(\partial(S^1\times D^2))\subset E_{P(K)}$ be the companion torus. Then $T_c$ is incompressible and is not boundary-parallel in $E_{P(K)}$; hence it is essential.

Assume full AC. Let $M=E_{P(K)}$ be a satellite knot exterior with companion torus $T_c$. Suppose the pattern hypotheses of the essential-companion-torus lemma hold, both components of $M$ cut along $T_c$ are atoroidal or Seifert-fibered, and $M$ itself is neither atoroidal nor Seifert-fibered. Then the inclusion-minimal JSJ system of $M$ consists of a torus ambient isotopic to $T_c$. Cutting along that torus identifies the companion exterior $E_K$ as the component on the outside of the embedded companion solid torus. No conclusion is made for an essential companion torus that is absorbed into a Seifert-fibered union.

Assume full AC. Let $K:S^1\to S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot with a chosen compact exterior $E_K$. Let $M$ be a compact connected orientable smooth Seifert-fibered three-manifold and let $T$ be a boundary torus whose inclusion induces an injection on fundamental groups. Fix one Seifert fibration and a based regular fiber $h\in\pi_1(T)\subset\pi_1(M)$. Suppose the quotient $\pi_1(M)/\langle h\rangle$ is isomorphic to a finite free product of at least two nontrivial groups, excluding the free product of two groups of order two. Then every Seifert fibration of $M$ has the same unoriented regular-fiber slope on $T$ as the fixed fibration. No choice hypothesis is introduced. The notation $\langle h\rangle$ denotes the cyclic subgroup, which is normal as proved below.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice as an ambient hypothesis; the finite construction and
the ODE interfaces below use no additional choice, so this hypothesis is
dispensable. A smooth manifold with corners here is Hausdorff and second
countable, with charts in relatively open subsets of $[0,\infty)^c\times\mathbb R^{n-c}$
and transition maps smoothly extendible with invertible derivative at corner
points; transitions preserve the local depth and its face germs. Let $M$ be
compact. Then $M$ has a finite corner-adapted whole-star smooth triangulation.
Corner faces are locally subpolyhedra, and any specified finite union of
closed faces is a subpolyhedron.

If the total boundary already has a finite piecewise smooth triangulation
$f:L\to\partial M$ compatible on all local face intersections, with its
differential fan giving a homeomorphism onto the union of boundary faces of the
tangent orthant at each point, the triangulation extends to $M$, pointwise
preserving $f$ with compatible subdivisions allowed. In the resulting finite
union construction all intersections may be made full subcomplexes. The same
relative conclusion applies to a fixed corner-adapted triangulated closed neighbourhood piece
whose smaller protected subcomplex lies in its relative interior: fitting is
performed away from that protected subcomplex. No extension of arbitrary
incompatible boundary data is asserted.

Let $G=G_1*\cdots*G_k$, where $2\le k<\infty$ and every factor is nontrivial. If $k=2$, assume the two factors are not both cyclic of order two. Then every cyclic normal subgroup of $G$ is trivial. No choice hypothesis is required.

derivations.claim: The circle action $t\cdot(z,w)=(e^{4\pi i t}z,e^{2\pi i t}w)$ on $S^1\times D^2$ has generic orbit slope $2\lambda_V+\mu_V$. The given pattern is one such orbit. The core $S^1\times\{0\}$ has stabilizer of order $2$, while generic points have trivial stabilizer. Removing a tube about the regular orbit $P_{2,1}$ therefore gives a Seifert fibration of $X_{P_{2,1}}$ over an annulus with one exceptional point of multiplicity $2$. On the outer torus its regular-fiber slope is $2\lambda_V+\mu_V$.

Remove a small neighborhood of the exceptional point from the annulus base. The remaining pair of pants has fundamental group freely generated by a loop $a$ around the outer boundary and a loop $c$ around the removed cone point; its third boundary loop is $(ac)^{-1}$. The circle bundle over this pair of pants has a section: it retracts to a graph, and a section over that graph is obtained by choosing one point in the fiber at the vertex and extending over each edge. Thus its group has generators $a,c,h$, with $h$ the fiber and $[a,h]=[c,h]=1$. The order-two local model $(z,w)\mapsto(-z,-w)$ around the exceptional core identifies the filled meridian with $c^2h$ after replacing $c$ by $ch^k$ if necessary: one circuit of the cone-point boundary lifts from $(z,w)$ to $(-z,-w)$, so two circuits equal one inverse fiber turn, and the twisting coefficient is odd. Filling that neighborhood kills this meridian. By [F3],
$$
\pi_1(X_{P_{2,1}})=\langle a,c,h\mid [a,h]=[c,h]=1,\ c^2h=1\rangle.
$$
Its quotient by $\langle h\rangle$ is $\mathbb Z*C_2$, which is nonabelian by reduced normal forms [F4]; hence $X_{P_{2,1}}$ is not $T^2\times I$. Its outer boundary subgroup is generated by $a,h$. The abelianization is free on $[a],[c]$ with $[h]=-2[c]$, so $a^m h^n=1$ implies $m=0$ and $n=0$. Thus the outer torus group injects into $\pi_1(X_{P_{2,1}})$ and has no compressing disk.

For the trefoil, [F2] gives $\pi_1(E_K)=\langle x,y\mid x^2=y^3\rangle$ and regular fiber $h_K=x^2=y^3$. Its quotient by $\langle h_K\rangle$ is $C_2*C_3$, nonabelian by [F4], and $h_K$ is infinite because its abelianization is $6$ times the generator of $H_1(E_K)\cong\mathbb Z$. The group maps onto $S_3$ by $x\mapsto(12)$ and $y\mapsto(123)$, so it is nonabelian and $K$ is not the unknot, whose exterior group is $\mathbb Z$.

The peripheral formula in [F2] gives $h_K=\lambda_K+6\mu_K$. The companion embedding identifies $(\mu_V,\lambda_V)$ with $(\mu_K,\lambda_K)$. Therefore the two Seifert fibrations on the cut sides induce slopes $2\lambda+\mu$ and $\lambda+6\mu$ on the companion torus. Their determinant in the ordered basis $(\mu,\lambda)$ is $\det\begin{pmatrix}1&6\\2&1\end{pmatrix}=-11$, so the slopes are not parallel.
By [F7], the companion torus $T_c$ is essential. Hence the whole exterior $M=E_{P_{2,1}(K)}$ is not atoroidal. Both pieces cut along $T_c$ are Seifert-fibered by steps 1.1 and 1.3.

The horizontal case is impossible. The interval-bundle bases inherit smooth transverse charts from the horizontal surface and the fiber charts. For any such compact connected surface with nonempty boundary, [F10] gives a finite triangulation. Root a spanning tree of its triangle-adjacency graph at a boundary edge. Delete each triangle across its exposed parent edge, starting at the root; this collapses the surface to a finite connected graph. Its group is therefore free, with rank equal to the rank of its abelianization, by collapsing a graph spanning tree. For a closed surface, the polygon models of [F5] give abelianization $\mathbb Z^{2g}$ in the orientable genus $g$ case and $\mathbb Z^{k-1}\oplus\mathbb Z/2$ in the nonorientable genus $k$ case, by adding the signed edge occurrences in its single face word. Hence a compact surface group with torsion-free rank-two abelianization is either the torus group $\mathbb Z^2$ or the free group of rank two; with torsion-free rank-one abelianization it is infinite cyclic. The cable group has abelianization $\mathbb Z^2$, is nonabelian because its quotient is $\mathbb Z*C_2$, and has the nonidentity central element $h$ since $[h]=-2[c]$ in its abelianization. It is neither $\mathbb Z^2$ nor the free group of rank two, whose center is trivial by [F11]. The trefoil group has abelianization $\mathbb Z$ and is nonabelian by step 1.3, so it too is not a surface group with that abelianization. Thus neither cut piece can be an interval bundle over a surface.

Suppose $M$ had a Seifert fibration. It is irreducible by [[lem-knot-exterior-is-irreducible]], so [F6] makes $T_c$ ambient isotopic to a vertical or horizontal torus. Isotopy preserves the homeomorphism types of the cut pieces. In the horizontal case, cutting along $T_c$ gives interval bundles over compact connected surfaces, so each side group is a surface group.

Suppose instead that $T_c$ is vertical after isotopy. Pull the hypothetical fibration back by that ambient isotopy, so the original $T_c$ is vertical and the original cut-piece markings are retained. Restriction gives a Seifert fibration on each cut piece with one common regular-fiber slope on $T_c$. Their boundary groups inject independently of any general knot-boundary incompressibility theorem. For the cable side this was proved in step 1.2. For the trefoil side, the peripheral formula of [F2], with $2(-1)+3(1)=1$, gives $\mu=y^{-1}x$ and $\lambda=h_K\mu^{-6}$. Thus $(\mu,h_K)$ is also a basis for its boundary-torus group. In the quotient $C_2*C_3$ the word $y^{-1}x$ is cyclically reduced of length two, so all its nonzero powers are nonidentity by [F4]. If $\mu^a h_K^b=1$, quotienting forces $a=0$, and the infinite order of $h_K$ from step 1.3 forces $b=0$. This proves injectivity of that boundary group. The two original fiber quotients are $\mathbb Z*C_2$ and $C_2*C_3$, respectively, by steps 1.2 and 1.3; neither is the two-order-two exception. Apply [F9] separately to the restricted hypothetical fibration on each side. Its common boundary-fiber slope must equal both original slopes, contradicting their determinant $-11$ in step 2.1. This rules out the vertical case; together with step 2.3 it proves that $M$ is not Seifert-fibered.

Steps 2.2 and 4.1 verify the nonamalgamation hypotheses of [F8], so the companion torus is a JSJ torus and the component outside the companion solid torus is $E_K$. The smooth ambient uniqueness in [F8] carries the original marked outside component to the outside component for any isotopic minimal JSJ torus.
